newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends weaker in US, sterling gains pared.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends weaker in US, sterling gains pared.

text.p: The dollar ended broadly lower in U.S. trading on Tuesday, weakening against the mark and the Swiss franc after Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said he would not welcome further dollar strength.
The dollar had pushed higher at the outset of trading following bullish forecasts for U.S. economic growth from the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM).
But it turned lower on the Welteke remarks, then traded just above its session-troughs for the remainder of the day.
The greenback ended at 1.7240/50 marks versus 1.7300/05 at the open, and edged down to 125.35/40 yen against 125.62/72.

"The German comments knocked us back," said Robert Sabia, vice president at ING Barings Capital Markets. "Sterling/mark buying got dollar/mark back above 1.73 but once we fell through 1.7260 it became a dump session."

Speaking to reporters on the fringes of a meeting of Germany's IG Metall trade union, Welteke said that the appreciation of the dollar in recent months had led to a slight rise in German import prices, which could have a delayed impact on producer and later on consumer prices.
"Because of this we cannot welcome a further rise in the dollar," Welteke said.
Following the remarks traders sold the dollar, which has risen by roughly 12 percent against the mark since the beginning of the year, pushing it to a session low of 1.7195.
Dealers said the market appeared hesitant to go long dollars for the remainder of the day, but predicted little additional near-term damage.
"As long as we don't go below 1.7150 I don't think there's any reason to sell dollars," said Hans Boman, Swedbank's chief spot dealer. "Fundamentally it's still pointing straight up."

On Tuesday however, dollar bulls took a breather. A rally in Japanese stocks and a climb in Japanese market interest rates fueled buying of yen overnight and kept the yen well-bid during U.S. trade. The Nikkei share average rose 666.17 points or 3.41 percent, to finish at 20,180.92, its highest closing level since December 17. The yield on the benchmark bond rose as high as 2.425 percent, up from 2.300 percent on Friday.

"The appreciation of the yen started last night as a knee-jerk reaction to the Nikkei gaining over three percent and long-term interest rates ticking back up," said ING's Sabia. "Everyone saw that as a reason to purchase yen."

In other trade, sterling ended modestly weaker against the dollar after soaring overseas on news that new British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown had raised rates 25 basis points and moved to give the Bank of England full independence in setting monetary policy.
"The market was shocked about the speed with which the new Labour government acted," said Bob Savage, chief foreign exchange dealer at Lehman Brothers.
"The most surprising news was making the Bank of England independent which has made the inflation fight in the UK a credible one and changed the playing field for sterling."
The pound ended the session at $1.6328/35, down from $1.6350/60 at the open.
In tandem with its fall against the mark, the dollar weakened to 1.4620/30 Swiss francs against 1.4710/20 at the outset of trading.
The greenback edged up to Canadian $1.3780/85 from C$1.3770/75, while the Australian dollar closed at $0.7764/69, slightly lower than its opening rate of $0.7767/72.
